description: ASTRIXFORGE is a team motivated by curiosity, creativity, and a love of technology. We are enthusiastic about investigating the interesting facts and mysteries of space, gaining a better understanding of our universe, and applying technology in order to turn ideas into practical solutions
summary:
MICRO//FLAME is an educational research tool focusing on the combustion in microgravity and importance of fire safety within spacecraft. Due to buoyancy on Earth the shape of the flames and airflow are altered however by reducing buoyancy in microgravity scientists can test combustion in different ways.

All of this information is presented clearly on the website. The 3D Combustion Lab can be used to manipulate factors such as the oxygen levels, temperature, gravity and fuel shape. This can be viewed in a display showing how it affects the flame. The Spacecraft Material Inspector shows what materials there are and how they relate to igniting, flame spread and extinguishing. The knowledge graph will show how the ideas connect, such as combustion, materials, experiments, where experiments are carried out and safety concerns.

MICRO//FLAME also contains a NASA Research Vault, Evidence Explorer and research console to view results from programs such as ACME, SoFIE, FLEX, BASS and Saffire. A virtual Mission Lab and 3D scenes can also be used to view how the experiments were set up.

This project makes complex research easier to understand through explanation, visual models and sources. The simulations are for educational purposes only and aren’t for calculations or using in spacecraft safety. By connecting scientific concepts with NASA research MICRO//FLAME can help people learn about combustion and improve space travel in the future.
details:
# MICRO//FLAME - Flame without buoyancy

Team Name: ASTRIXFORGE Team Members: Malemnganba Laitonjam and Aashkar Haider Project Title: Microgravity Combustion Research Interface

1. What does your project do?

MICRO//FLAME is an interactive educational resource which allows you to learn about how fire works in microgravity and the importance of studying combustion in space.

When on earth, hot gasses will rise due to gravity creating buoyant airflow around flames. However in microgravity this effect is greatly diminished meaning you can analyse other factors such as diffusion, oxygen content, heat transfer and radiation.

Our website contains six different features to showcase the science behind this:

Flame Simulation: You can change variables such as fuel diameter, oxygen content, temperature, gravity and chamber pressure to see how it affects the example flame.

Materials: Information on materials used in spacecraft and the importance of this in regards to fire.

Knowledge Network: This shows links between combustion physics, experiments, research centres and spacecraft safety.

Combustion Trends: You can view educational combustion trends.

NASA Research Centre: View NASA and NASA Technical Reports Server (NTRS) research.

Fire Insights: Contains evidence explorer, research tools and mission simulations.

2. What are the benefits of your project?

MICRO//FLAME has been created to help people understand complex scientific information using interactive visualisation tools.

The main benefits include:

Helps students understand the differences between combustion on earth and in microgravity.

Interactive models allow people to enjoy learning about scientific concepts.

All NASA research and scientific information is organised.

Helps you learn about spacecraft fire safety and materials.

Encourages curiosity in science and self researching.

Helps users learn about how different parameters affect combustion.

3. What impact do you hope to have?

The purpose of our project is to help people understand the science behind microgravity combustion.

This will help increase people’s awareness of the challenges that come along with fire safety in spacecraft.

Ultimately we hope that MICRO//FLAME encourages more students to get into science, engineering, coding and space research.

It is simply an educational website. It is not a validated CFD solver or a certified system for analysing spacecraft fire risk.

4. What technology, coding languages or hardware did you use?

We created our website using web technologies and visualisation tools.

Languages and technologies:

HTML: Used to create the structure of our website.

CSS: Used to design the layout, style, colour scheme and responsive design.

JavaScript: Used to create interactive elements, simulations, navigation and visualisations.

Canvas & SVG: Used to create custom graphics.

Software:

Spline: Used to create an interactive 3D scene.

Anime.js: Used to create animations throughout the interface.

Web Browser: Used to run the website.

NASA & NTRS Websites: Used as scientific references.

AI Tools (Optional): The website contains configurable options to link to AI tools such as Google Gemini and Manus.

Hardware: We used a computer to create and test our website. There is no specialised scientific or lab equipment required to create an educational website.

5. How creative is your project?

MICRO//FLAME is very creative as it takes scientific research and combines it with interactive learning and 3D visuals to create a modern website.

Rather than just paragraphs of information and static diagrams, we have allowed users to play around with variables to see how they affect the educational flame.

We have linked the scientific concepts to research done by NASA, material information, knowledge networks and mission simulations.

The dark futuristic theme and cyan colour scheme was chosen to give a feel of space research. Everything has been organised so the information is easy to understand.

6. What have you considered?

While creating MICRO//FLAME, we took into consideration:

Scientific: The information provided should be related to real scientific research into microgravity combustion and known NASA research.

Educational: The website should be easy to understand and useful for students and beginners.

Navigation: The website has easy to navigate interactive elements.

Visual: 3D elements, charts and effects have been added to help explain complex concepts.

Accessibility: It can be accessed using a web browser and is responsive to different screen sizes.

Scientific References: Where possible the scientific information has been linked to reliable references.

Responsible: We have made it clear what is a simulation for educational purposes and what would be actual measurements taken from experiments and validated predictions.

Expandable: There are optional AI tools and extra research tools which can be configured.

Conclusion

Overall, we have tried to combine space science with interactive technology. ASTRIXFORGE hopes to make it easier to understand microgravity combustion, encourage learning in science and increase awareness of fire safety in future space missions.

Created by: Malemnganba Laitonjam and Aashkar Haider
